sentence_of_record: LEAF-POWERED (2026-09-14, 2,150 single-order verdicts): PRIMARY FAIL (pooled anchor 0.934 vs leaf 0.931, -0.003, 9:7, p = 0.80; no anchor significant under Holm), and for a reason that settles the leaf layer: the arms give an identical verdict on 92.9% of all 1,078 matches, and of the 786 key-decidable ones only 16 (2.0%) differ in whether the verdict was CORRECT, so the rubric moves verdicts but almost never across the right/wrong boundary; the arithmetic ceiling on a leaf rubric's effect is +-2pp and the earlier 6-17pp per-anchor 'gains' were noise. Registered power assumed a 0.10 discordant rate; the observed 0.02 means it could not have detected 6pp as a significance test, but the low discordance IS the measurement. Scope: leaf vs ANCHOR, both domain-specific; the 0.93 figures are single-order and filtered.

plain_description.what: About 2,150 verdicts on four subject areas, comparing the judge using a grading guide written for each fine-grained leaf of the tree with the judge using a guide written for the broad subject.
plain_description.why: It tests whether making the judge's instructions more specific to each cell improves its accuracy.
plain_description.information: A gain would support cell-specific judging. No gain would close that line. Result: done. No gain: 0.934 with the broad guide against 0.931 with the leaf guide. The two guides give the same verdict on 93% of matches and change right-or-wrong on only 2% of the decidable ones, so a leaf guide can move accuracy by at most about 2 points. Earlier larger per-subject 'gains' were noise. This was single-order judging on filtered matches, and it compares leaf against subject guides only. Later ruled history rather than evidence, because it ran on the older question pool.
